\Section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:evaluation}

The evaluation asks what the mechanical component adds to an agent, in completeness and in cost, and whether it changes which model is needed.
\emph{Arm against arm} (Sec.~\ref{sec:eval-arms}) holds the model fixed and varies the tactic: \textit{agent-only}, \textit{hybrid-guided}, and \textit{hybrid-flexible}, run under the same conditions.
\emph{Model against model} (Sec.~\ref{sec:eval-models}) repeats the design under a frontier model and a mid-tier model of the same family and asks whether, with \WP, the cheaper model reaches the results of the frontier model.
Both rounds share the corpus, the protocol, the scoring, and the cost accounting described first.

\SubSection{Setup}
\label{sec:eval-setup}

\Paragraph{Corpus}
The corpus has 26 targets from 12 modules.
Twenty-four are extracted from public Move code of the Aptos framework at a pinned commit: ten from its experimental trading modules, thirteen from modules for accounts, authentication, and rate and stake limits, and one from the Move standard library.
The other two are written for the corpus.
Function bodies are copied unchanged except for a few reductions documented in the module headers, and the package includes everything the targets depend on.
No target has a specification upstream.
A model may have seen the code during training, but it cannot recall a contract that was never written, so it has to infer one.
Every target is classified by the features (strata) its contract has to account for --- loops, early returns and breaks, arithmetic overflow and underflow, options and enums, global state, tables and maps, mutable references and in-place permutation, function values, quantifiers, composition through a callee's contract, and others, 32 in all.
Thirteen targets have a loop that needs an invariant, and three are deliberately guessable as controls.
Each target has a hand-written reference specification that proves within 20 seconds, and six \emph{mutants} in two disjoint sets of three --- patches to the implementation, one per obligation the contract has to pin --- each shown to be killed by the reference.
A task starts from the package with the reference contracts of every function the target calls; the contracts of the target and of all other functions are withheld, since a caller's contract can restate what the target does.
With 3 arms and 4 replicates, a model round has \textbf{312 cells}.

\Paragraph{Arms and models}
The three tactics of Sec.~\ref{sec:skills} run as arms that differ only in the rendered plugin: the reference material is byte-identical, and in agent-only the \WP tool is absent rather than discouraged.
Two rounds use two models of one family through the same runtime, the Codex CLI at high effort: Sol~5.6, the frontier model, and Terra~5.6, the mid-tier model, priced at about half of Sol's list price.
Each session has a budget of 100k output tokens, one hour of wall time, and 40 seconds of solver time per verification condition.

\Paragraph{Scoring}
A cell reaches \emph{operational success} when a judge outside the agent's workspace confirms that the package compiles, the requested scope verifies, no weakening construct is present --- |pragma verify = false|, partial abort contracts, vacuous postconditions, invented preconditions --- the bytecode is unchanged, and the required contract categories are present.
The agent's own claim is never a score, and the agent receives only this acceptance feedback: the mutants are withheld until generation has ended, and a contract is never handed back for strengthening.
Operational success is necessary but weak: a vaguer contract passes it more easily.
Completeness --- postconditions as strong as the behavior --- has no deductive check in general; \WP guarantees it only given complete loop invariants and callee contracts.
The second level is therefore \emph{mutation adequacy}: after the round, each withheld mutant is applied to the implementation, and the prover is rerun against the inferred specification.
A cell is \emph{complete} when its specification kills all six mutants and \emph{failed} when one survives; a cell in which a mutant reached no verdict within the solver's time limit is \emph{unmeasured}.
All 624 cells reached operational success, so the outcome of a cell is decided by the withheld mutants alone.

\Paragraph{Cost accounting}
Costs are in US dollars at each model's published list prices, computed from the recorded token counters of every model request; startup requests that do no task work are excluded.
Per million tokens, Sol~5.6 is \$4 uncached input, \$0.40 cached input, and \$20 output; Terra~5.6 is \$2, \$0.20, and \$12.
Thinking counts as output for both.
Means are task-weighted, and the 95\% intervals are percentile bootstraps over the 26 tasks (10,000 resamples).
Differences in completeness are tested with the preregistered blocked randomization tests of the round analysis, Holm-adjusted.

\Paragraph{Cost}
Under both models the hybrids cost less than agent-only: 0.86$\times$ and 0.87$\times$ under Sol~5.6 and 0.79$\times$ and 0.89$\times$ under Terra~5.6 (hybrid-guided, hybrid-flexible).
Over all targets, only the interval of Sol's hybrid-flexible excludes parity, but the targets split into two clear groups.
On the 13 targets without a loop that needs an invariant, \WP derives the complete contract and the agent only has to check it: the hybrids cost 0.36--0.60$\times$ agent-only, and every interval lies below 0.75.
On the 13 loop targets they cost 1.09--1.22$\times$: the agent still has to find the invariant, and the quantified \WP output adds to the context it re-reads on every turn.
Overall the hybrids read less input than agent-only (288k and 280k against 333k tokens per cell under Sol~5.6, 289k and 335k against 367k under Terra~5.6) and write less output.

\Paragraph{Completeness}
The tactics do not change completeness measurably: under both models, both preregistered contrasts have Holm $p = 1.00$.
Agent-only completes 103 of 104 cells under Sol~5.6 and 97 under Terra~5.6, the hybrids 98 and 98, and 97 and 98.
All failures but one Terra~5.6 agent-only cell occur on three loop targets.
|partition|, an in-place partition, is the one target whose contract needs a permutation argument proved with lemmas; it fails in every arm, and in every failure a mutant that overwrites an element instead of swapping it survives: the contract does not state that the result is a rearrangement of the input.
On the two scans |upsert_provider_jwks| and |cancel_at_price_level|, which leave the loop early, only hybrid cells fail (5 under Sol~5.6, 6 under Terra~5.6): the agent added invariants for the scanned prefix, accepted the quantified contract that \WP derived from them once it verified, and a withheld mutant on the exit path survived.
The hybrids do improve the first attempt: the share of cells whose first candidate check is accepted rises from 62\% to 68--71\% under Sol~5.6 and from 37\% to 63--65\% under Terra~5.6, and rejected checks drop from 66 to 40--60 and from 117 to 66--82.

\SubSection{Model against Model}
\label{sec:eval-models}

Terra~5.6 costs 0.57$\times$ Sol~5.6 under agent-only and 0.53$\times$ and 0.59$\times$ under the hybrids, with all intervals within [0.45, 0.65], and it is cheaper on 25 or 26 of the 26 targets in every arm.
These ratios are close to the price ratio of 0.5 for input and 0.6 for output: the two models spend about the same number of tokens per cell, Terra~5.6 up to a fifth more input, and Terra~5.6 is slower (143--153 against 115--126 seconds).
Completeness differs on one target.
Outside |partition|, Terra~5.6 fails one agent-only cell and, under the hybrids, the same two scans as Sol~5.6; on the partition it fails 10 of 12 cells, Sol~5.6 3 of 12.
The frontier model's advantage is therefore the lemma-based permutation argument, not the loop invariants, compositions, and global state that make up the rest of the corpus.
The one target on which Terra~5.6 costs about as much as Sol~5.6 is |select|, whose contract needs a recursive specification function over a function value; there it writes 1.5--2.0$\times$ Sol's output.
With \WP, Terra's first-check acceptance (63--65\%) approaches Sol's (68--71\%), and Terra~5.6 under hybrid-guided completes 97 of 104 cells at 46\% of the cost of Sol~5.6 under agent-only, which completes 103.
